title: Stricter fireworks rules and year-round boulevard parking
subtitle: Anti-harassment legislation support, Mill Street and King Street East developments, Vision Zero upgrades, and land purchase
overview: Council tightened the fireworks by-law {{vote:m1}}. Displays are now limited to the day of celebration (Victoria Day, Canada Day and Diwali) and must end by 11pm. A proposal to add Lunar New Year was defeated, and delegates from the fireworks industry asked for rain dates and more consultation.

Council also approved year-round parking on paved driveway boulevards under a set of conditions, including a rule that vehicles in school zones be removed before 8 a.m. on weekdays. It unanimously endorsed Ontario Big City Mayors' call for provincial legislation to strengthen municipal codes of conduct and address council harassment {{vote:m2}}.

On development, council approved land-use changes for mixed-use projects at 455-509 Mill Street and 1001 King Street East, accepted Vision Zero road-safety improvements, and asked staff to consider financial incentives for missing middle and affordable housing. After a closed session, council authorized acquiring 470 King Street East for a community facility. Council also appointed Councillor A. Owodunni to the Economic Development Advisory Committee in place of Councillor P. Singh.

decisions.detail: Council limited fireworks to the day of celebration (Victoria Day, Canada Day, Diwali) ending by 11pm and repealed and replaced the fireworks chapters of the Municipal Code {{vote:m1}}.
Council backed the Ontario Big City Mayors resolution asking the province to strengthen municipal codes of conduct and enforcement, including support for Bill 5 {{vote:m2}}.
Parking on paved driveway boulevards is permitted year-round under conditions such as keeping off landscaping, staying 15 metres from intersections, and clearing school zones by 8 a.m. on weekdays.

decisions.item: Vision Zero progress and hot spots
decisions.detail: Council received the 2022 Vision Zero progress update and directed staff to implement the proposed hot spot road-safety improvements.
Council will use the feasibility study to inform planning work and directed staff to consider financial incentives and report back once more is known about Bill 23.
Council adopted an Official Plan amendment and approved rezoning to allow a high-intensity mixed-use development, changing the land from general industrial employment.
Council adopted an Official Plan amendment and approved rezoning to permit a mixed-use development and adopted the urban design brief.
Following the closed session, council authorized acquiring 470 King Street East, with the Mayor and Clerk to sign the necessary documents.

debate: Two fireworks delegates, an industry association representative and a retailer, supported the 11pm cut-off but opposed removing the day before and day after, saying a single day leaves no rain or high-wind option and could lead to people storing unused fireworks at home. They also said the staff report lacked complaint details and consultation evidence, and urged education and vendor training rather than tighter limits.

Some councillors argued that behaviour problems, such as fireworks late at night, extend beyond a small minority and that the new rules should be given time to work. One said education and a trial period were preferable to more exceptions.

On adding Lunar New Year, supporters pointed to a written request from a Chinese Canadian association, the size of that community, and that neighbouring municipalities already allow it. They also cited consistency with Diwali being permitted. Opponents worried that adding one celebration would invite requests from many other groups and increase by-law enforcement workload. Staff had no strong view and noted the holiday lasts about two weeks.

A delegate for a women's advocacy group urged support for Bill 5, saying municipal councillors face no workplace harassment accountability comparable to other jobs. Councillors who spoke agreed, and the Mayor said the OBCM wording leaves room for the province to fold the measures into government legislation.

During questions, councillors raised illegal signs on boulevards. Staff said many are tied to out-of-town cell numbers, which makes charging anyone difficult, and that all staff have been asked to collect them. Staff advised residents not to remove signs themselves.
